profiles.name: Personal & Professional Development
profiles.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

profiles.name: Introduction to Economics
profiles.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
profiles.profile: This course provides an introduction to the principles of economics. The first part of the course delves into microeconomics concepts, including supply and demand, game theory, theory of consumer behaviour, theory of the firm and market structure. The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.
profiles.topics: game theory; theory of consumer behaviour; theory of the firm; market structure; aggregate output; inflation rate

profiles.name: International Macroeconomics
profiles.description2: Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
profiles.profile: This course explores the economy as a whole by examining its dynamics over the short, medium, and long run. Key indicators such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment are studied. The course analyses how fiscal and monetary polici es affect the economy. It also covers business cycles, economic crises, and international trade, providing the tools needed to interpret economic data, evaluate policy decisions, and understand global economic trends.

profiles.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
profiles.description2: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
profiles.profile: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of advanced topics in microeconomic theory. Structured in three parts, the course begins with an in-depth analysis of consumer behaviour, including decision-making under uncertainty, non -egoistic preferences, and cognitive limitations. The second part analyses market structures with an emphasis on imperfect competition, strategic behaviour, and the functioning of factor markets. The final part of the course covers general equilibrium and market efficiency, investigating externalities and the role of government in the economy. Throughout the course, students will engage with research papers through presentations and discussions, bridging theoretical concepts with empirical evidence.
profiles.topics: decision-making under uncertainty; non -egoistic preferences; cognitive limitations; general equilibrium; market efficiency; investigating externalities

profiles.name: Public Economics
profiles.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.

profiles.name: Econometrics
profiles.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

profiles.name: Behavioral Economics
profiles.description2: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.

profiles.name: Research Methods & Statistics
profiles.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
profiles.profile: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
profiles.topics: research design; operationalization; sampling; experiments; surveys; descriptive and inferential statistics

profiles.name: Introduction to Data Science
profiles.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
profiles.profile: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.

profiles.name: Machine Learning
profiles.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
profiles.profile: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.

profiles.name: Mathematical Methods
profiles.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
profiles.profile: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3

profiles.name: Building with Nature
profiles.description2: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.
profiles.profile: Building, or the construction of man-made structures, would seem to be at odds with nature. One is shaped over time by natural forces, while the other makes changes to suit our specific human needs at a given time. However, to truly stand the test of time human structures, and thus to some degree civilisation, must work with nature and not in spite of it, or even against it. In this course we will explore different aspects of Building with Nature, with special interest in those aspects of Zeeland where this approach has been implemented. We will also explore a bit of the history of Walcheren to better understand what situations its people have already overcome, when facing the sea. Furthermore, we will look at how better planning and engineering is allowing nature to maintain, or even regain, vital ecosystem health across the globe. How can we learn from nature and utilise the forces at work to our mutual benefit? How can we make space for ourselves without disrupting key habitat features animals depend on to thrive?
profiles.topics: ecosystem based design; land reclamation; flood protection; guest lectures; sustainable engineering; excursions

profiles.name: Living with Water
profiles.description2: Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure.
profiles.profile: Delta regions around the world face growing challenges related to sea-level rise, flooding, freshwater scarcity, land subsidence, and unequal access to water and protection. At the same time, these regions are home to millions of people whose lives are shaped by water. This course explores how societies in delta regions manage water risks and opportunities, with a particular focus on the Dutch province of Zeeland as a living laboratory. Students are introduced to key concepts in sustainable water management, including flood protection, drainage and freshwater management, salinization, land subsidence, the ecological consequences of water infrastructure, and the social dimensions of water governance. The course examines how historical events have shaped contemporary approaches to water management, and how governance structures, laws, and institutions influence decisions about safety, land use, sustainability, and whose interests are prioritized. Throughout the course, emphasis is placed on the idea of adapting to water dynamics through integrated strategies, nature-based solutions, and resilient planning, while critically reflecting on questions of long-term social impacts. Learning takes place through a combination of assigned readings, short lectures, group discussions, and in-class activities that encourage critical reflection and collaborative learning. Students engage with real-world cases through guest speakers from policy and research, as well as excursions and field-based activities in Zeeland when possible.
profiles.topics: flood protection; freshwater management; land subsidence; ecological consequences of water infrastructure; social dimensions of water governance; highlights nature based

profiles.name: Governance of Sustainability
profiles.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions. The first part of this course introduces you to the basic conceptual tools for understanding governance and to the major fault line in tackling sustainability problems as identified by Charles Mann in “The Wizard and the Prophet”. Wizards are techno-optimists who believe humanity’s creativity can tackle every challenge, whilst Prophets argue that humans should take a holistic and systemic approach that calls for a drastic reduction of exploiting the earth resources to respect planetary boundaries. In the second part of the course, we use Problem Based Learning to examine governance solutions to concrete sustainability challenges regarding food, freshwater, energy, and climate change.

profiles.name: Introduction to Biodiversity
profiles.description2: The first part of this course introduces you to the basic conceptual tools for understanding governance and to the major fault line in tackling sustainability problems as identified by Charles Mann in “The Wizard and the Prophet”. Wizards are techno-optimists who believe humanity’s creativity can tackle each and every challenge, whilst Prophets argue that humans should take a holistic and systemic approach that calls for a drastic reduction of exploiting the earth resources in order to respect planetary boundaries.
profiles.profile: The biosphere consists of millions of living species, and millions more have existed in the past. The total number of living species is still unknown, but current developments in palaeontology, molecular biology, and sampling techniques, have reshaped our view of the classification of the living world. It is now recognized that plants and animals; traditionally the two groups defining the science of biology, are merely two branches on a giant tree of life. Many other independent and diverse groups exist, such as brown algae, fungi, diatoms, archaea and many different groups of bacteria. The aim of this course is two-fold. Firstly, it will provide an overview of the living world. We will travel through the tree of life, starting with the prokaryote domains of bacteria and archaea. We will investigate different prokaryote groups, their ways of life, and their manifestations in the world around us. Next, we will explore the diversity of eukaryotes. There are countless single-celled eukaryotic groups that play important ecological roles, such as dinoflagellates that help create coral reefs, and apicomplexans that cause diseases like malaria. Finally, we will discuss the multicellular groups that shape the world around us: plants, seaweeds, fungi and animals. Methods for investigating biodiversity will also be discussed. The second aim of this course is to investigate the relevance of biodiversity for human society. There are multiple number domains in which biodiversity is important, i.e.

profiles.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
profiles.description2: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.
profiles.profile: Ecology is the scientific study of the distribution and abundance of organisms and the interactions that determine distribution and abundance. Over the past decades, ecology has grown from an obscure science into a position at the forefront of public and political consciousness. Applied ecology has become an important scientific tool to address important political and environmental issues. Ecology is generally divided into 3 levels: the individual organism, the population (consisting of individuals of the same species) and the community, in which several species are living together. In addition, ecology focuses on the relationship between living creatures and their chemical and physical surroundings, which together make up an ecosystem. Ecology is a complex science. It draws on many areas of knowledge such as organic and inorganic chemistry, plant and animal biology, physiology, meteorology, and even economics. This course focuses on the basic principles of ecology, from individuals to ecosystems. We then proceed to environmental conditions and resources, and the 4 levels of ecology: individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems. Two weeks will be spent on ecological modelling, as an important tool for understanding and predicting ecological systems. We will conclude with some actual cases of applied ecology.

profiles.name: Dynamic Earth
profiles.description2: Introduces Earth Science by focusing on interactions among the deep earth, lithosphere and hydrosphere. Highlights key cycles shaping Earth’s surface and includes indoor/outdoor labs and a multi‑day field excursion.
profiles.profile: This course introduces you to the broad field of Earth Science. Earth Science in general and in all its sub disciplines is a very exciting and relevant field. You will never look at mountains, rivers and oceans in the same way after taking this course. You will discover in this course that many of the natural phenomena observed on (surface) and in (deep) the earth, are linked to processes of our Earth, that contrary to many other planets, is alive! The number of opportunities for employment in this field is increasing, because water, soil, mineral and fossil resources are limited. To limit the environmental impacts of our human endeavors new approaches are needed to counter water-soil-air pollution. Also, more efforts are needed to address the effects of the seemingly increased frequency of earthquakes, flooding, tsunamis and hurricanes. While studying the common geological phenomena, we will browse through major sub disciplines such as structural geology, mineralogy, petrology, earth history, geochemistry, geophysics, climatology, environmental geology, geohydrology, sedimentology, and resource management. Each one of these sub disciplines could easily fill a semester. At universities these sub-disciplines are usually taught by several professors that have specialized in one of the sub-disciplines. This course will be taught by professors partly based on the main division in Earth Science (surface earth disciplines) and Geophysics. Since geology is a typical outdoor science, you will not have a complete introduction without outdoor studies.

profiles.profile: This course serves as a 200-level elective within the Environmental Science unit of the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. Geospatial data and images from satellites or drones are widely used to explore and model changes in the Earth’s system at various scales. This course focused on hands-on experience with GIS and data integration techniques. We will explore, visualize, and analyze how human actions can impact global ecosystems and climate, and how tools like ArcGIS pro can promote sustainable practices like soil/water governance and coastal protection planning by combining data from different fields. This course includes practical exercises, a final exam and a case study based on earth science-focused research question.

profiles.name: Sustainability Essentials I
profiles.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
profiles.profile: ENSGATE101 - Sustainability Essentials serves as the Gateway course to all 200 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy all 200 level course in the cluster. We will use the model of planetary boundaries to discuss the concepts of sustainability with an anthropogenic focus. The planetary boundaries concept was presented in 2009 and provides a novel synthesis of the most pertinent global environmental challenges by analysing the risk of crossing critical thresholds in the behaviour of the Earth system’s processes. These boundaries act as a framework to define a "safe operating space for humanity," highlighting the limits within which human development can occur without causing catastrophic harm to the planet. 3

profiles.name: Climate Change
profiles.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
profiles.profile: Climate change is the defining challenge of our time. It has large impacts on both the living and non-living Earth systems, as well as drives a number of profound societal transformations. This course is roughly divided in 3 parts. First, we will first focus on the drivers of anthropogenic climate change and its impacts on the natural world. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) the properties of greenhouse gases, sea level rise, ocean acidification, climate feedback loops and effects on various biome types. Secondly, we will discuss impacts on various aspects of society. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) food production, transportation, construction, health, and migration patterns. We will discuss climate governance and -justice. We will also look at the history of the climate change debate and identify strategies that have been deployed by interest groups to sow doubt and misinformation. Lastly, we will look into solutions for both adaptation and mitigation, such as renewable energy systems, carbon dioxide storage and climate-adaptive spatial planning. The course will include a number of guest lectures and excursions. After taking the course, you will be able to explain the fundamentals of climate change science. You will also be able to navigate a vast flow of information on climate change, and identify main and reliable sources; you will have insight in main climate change issues and have an overview of the pathways to mitigation and adaptation.
